title: Cleveland v. Commissioner
articleTitle: Analytical Review of Cleveland v. Commissioner and Modern Standards for Qualified Research Activities
court: United States Court of Appeals, Fourth Circuit
subject: Trade or Business Requirement for Joint Venture Research
summary: Cleveland v. Commissioner, 297 F.2d 169 (4th Cir. 1961), governs when U.S. taxpayers financing an inventor's research may deduct research and experimental expenditures under IRC § 174. The Fourth Circuit held that advances made before the April 20, 1956 joint venture agreement were nondeductible loans, the backdated "as of" clause had no retroactive effect, and later experimental expenditures were deductible.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Background

The landmark decision by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit in Cleveland v. Commissioner, 297 F.2d 169 (4th Cir. 1961), affirming in part, reversing in part, and remanding the United States Tax Court's ruling in Cleveland v. Commissioner, 34 T.C. 517 (1960), establishes the foundational legal parameters governing when an investor or co-developer transitions from a passive creditor into an active joint venturer capable of deducting research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). Decided on December 7, 1961, by Circuit Judge Boreman (joined by Circuit Judges Soper and Haynsworth), the appellate ruling directly addresses the intersection of federal partnership taxation, contract retroactivity, and statutory research incentives within the jurisdiction of the United States.

The petitioners, Richard F. Cleveland and Jessie B. Cleveland, were husband and wife residing in Baltimore, Maryland, who filed joint federal income tax returns using the cash receipts and disbursements method of accounting for the taxable years 1955 and 1956. While Jessie B. Cleveland was a party to the litigation solely by virtue of filing joint returns, Richard F. Cleveland—a prominent practicing attorney in Baltimore—was the active taxpayer at the center of the controversy.

The dispute originated from a multi-decade relationship between Cleveland and Hans Kerla, a German immigrant, chemist, and inventor whom Cleveland first met in 1931 when Kerla sought legal advice. Over many years, Kerla had invented and worked to develop commercial applications for an inorganic liquid binder known as "Kerloid". Shortly after their initial meeting in the 1930s, Cleveland began advancing funds to Kerla both to support Kerla's family and to procure laboratory materials and equipment necessary to continue experimentation on the inorganic binder. To facilitate this work, Cleveland purchased a residential property in his own name in 1946, permitting Kerla to house his family rent-free while establishing a dedicated research laboratory in the building's large basement. Kerla also accessed laboratory facilities at Johns Hopkins University through professional associations with university faculty members and devoted his full time to the development of Kerloid during 1955 and 1956 and for a number of years prior thereto; Kerla died in September 1957.

Throughout this period, Cleveland was not merely a passive financier; although his primary vocation was the practice of law, he actively collaborated with Kerla to promote the Kerloid process commercially, acting as a business advisor, advising on the form of transactions transferring rights in the binder to users or prospective users, handling the related negotiations and legal documents, introducing Kerla to business contacts who might provide commercial outlets for the binder, and holding regular weekly conferences with Kerla to discuss the progress of the work. However, for more than twenty years, Cleveland and Kerla operated without any formal written contract defining their respective proprietary rights, repayment obligations, or business structure.

Following the enactment of Section 174 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954—which the Tax Court found Cleveland learned of sometime in 1954, although Cleveland testified that it was sometime in 1955—the parties sought to formalize their arrangement. On April 20, 1956, Cleveland and Kerla executed a formal written instrument styled as a "Trust Agreement," which explicitly purported to be effective retroactively "as of December 31, 1954". It was admitted that the primary purpose of the written agreement was to record the tenor of the parties' mutual understanding for purposes of IRC § 174(a)(1); Cleveland, the only witness at trial, testified that he had not wanted to put anything in writing earlier for fear of imposing undesirable restrictions on their commercial activities. Under the terms of the April 20, 1956 Trust Agreement, in consideration of Cleveland's advances through December 31, 1954 (recited as exceeding $68,700), Kerla agreed to hold the Kerloid invention, including present and future patents and patent applications, in trust one-half for himself and one-half for Cleveland, while retaining legal title and the right to prosecute patent applications in his own name as sole inventor; Cleveland confirmed that he had annually released Kerla from all claims for money advanced before January 1, 1955, and agreed to continue advancing the expenses of experimentation and Kerla's personal expenses to the extent of his reasonable financial ability; Kerla was not obligated to repay the experimental expenses but remained obligated to repay post-1954 advances for personal expenses only if fully able to do so; Kerla agreed to keep accurate annual records and submit an account to Cleveland by February 1 of each succeeding year; and the parties were to share equally in the avails of the invention, subject to commitments made to others.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Commissioner's Challenge

On their joint federal income tax returns, the Clevelands claimed deductions under IRC § 174(a)(1) for funds advanced to Kerla in the amounts of $5,598.42 for taxable year 1955 and $3,342.83 for taxable year 1956. Following an audit examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed the claimed R&E deductions in their entirety and issued statutory notices of deficiency in the amounts of $2,730.69 for 1955 and $1,571.13 for 1956.

While Cleveland and the Commissioner agreed that the amounts Kerla actually expended for research and experimental purposes were $4,923.07 in 1955 and $3,234.86 in 1956 (less than the amounts claimed, with no deduction claimed for advances Kerla used for personal living expenses), the Commissioner determined—and the Tax Court upheld—that the expenditures were not made by Cleveland in connection with his trade or business, a determination that turned on two fundamental legal questions. First, there was the question whether the outlays were "paid or incurred by the taxpayer": the Tax Court concluded that the advances were mere loans from which Kerla, not Cleveland, made the experimental expenditures, and that the written agreement merely converted the earlier loans into the purchase price paid by Cleveland for a one-half interest in Kerla's invention. Second, there was the "trade or business" nexus: the Tax Court found that Cleveland's primary occupation and business was the practice of law, and the Commissioner's determination, upheld by the Tax Court, was that the expenditures were not made "in connection with" a trade or business of Cleveland within the meaning of IRC § 174(a)(1).

In the initial trial proceeding (34 T.C. 517), Judge Withey of the United States Tax Court ruled entirely in favor of the Commissioner. The Tax Court found that Cleveland made no expenditures during the years at issue for experimental or developmental purposes, that he made the advances as mere loans from which Kerla, not Cleveland, made the experimental expenditures, and that the April 20, 1956 Trust Agreement created neither a partnership nor a joint venture, made no provision for sharing expenses and liabilities, and in prospective effect constituted no more than a sale by Kerla to Cleveland of a one-half interest in the invention in consideration of the moneys previously advanced, releasing Kerla from liability for their repayment.
Governing Statutory Framework and Modern R&D Tax Credit Nexus

The statutory centerpiece of Cleveland v. Commissioner is Section 174(a)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (26 U.S.C. § 174(a)(1)), which provided that a taxpayer may treat research or experimental expenditures which are paid or incurred by him during the taxable year in connection with his trade or business as expenses which are not chargeable to capital account, thereby allowing an immediate current deduction. Congress enacted Section 174 in 1954 specifically to eliminate the confusion and uncertainty of prior law—under which taxpayers lacking an established, ongoing business faced uncertainty as to whether product development costs could be currently deducted or instead had to be capitalized—and to stimulate the search for new products and inventions, particularly among small and growing enterprises.

Because Cleveland did not personally perform the bench chemistry, his entitlement to Section 174 treatment turned on whether he and Kerla were participants in a joint venture—a question the Fourth Circuit resolved under general joint venture principles and the Supreme Court's intent standard without citing Subchapter K of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC §§ 701, 702, 704, and 761), which defines a "partnership" for federal income tax purposes to include a syndicate, group, pool, joint venture, or other unincorporated organization through which any business, financial operation, or venture is carried on. Under the conduit rule of IRC § 702 and the Supreme Court's intent-based joint venture standard articulated in Commissioner v. Tower, 327 U.S. 280 (1946), and Commissioner v. Culbertson, 337 U.S. 733 (1949), if two parties form a bona fide joint venture in good faith and with a business purpose to conduct research and commercialize an invention, the venture's R&E expenditures flow through directly to the partners.

In contemporary United States tax practice, Cleveland v. Commissioner serves a dual statutory function across both R&E deduction regimes and the IRC § 41 Credit for Increasing Research Activities. For decades following Cleveland—and reinforced by the Supreme Court in Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), which granted certiorari specifically to resolve a circuit conflict between the Sixth Circuit and the Fourth Circuit's holding in Cleveland—Section 174 allowed immediate expensing of domestic R&E costs incurred "in connection with" a trade or business. Following the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) mandatory capitalization period for tax years 2022 through 2024 (which required five-year amortization for domestic R&E and fifteen-year amortization for foreign R&E under § 174), Congress enacted IRC § 174A in 2025, restoring current deductibility for domestic research and experimental expenditures for tax years beginning after 2024 while retaining fifteen-year amortization for foreign research under § 174. Both § 174 and § 174A retain the threshold requirement that expenditures be paid or incurred "in connection with" the taxpayer's trade or business.

Simultaneously, Cleveland governs the threshold gateway to the IRC § 41 Research Tax Credit. While Cleveland adjudicated deductions rather than credits, IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) explicitly incorporates the deduction standard as the first prong of the Four-Part Test, mandating that qualified research must consist of expenditures with respect to which outlays may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under Section 174 or Section 174A. However, Section 41 imposes a significantly narrower trade or business gateway under IRC § 41(b)(1): whereas Section 174/174A requires only that expenses be incurred "in connection with" a trade or business (permitting pre-revenue start-ups and joint ventures with a realistic prospect of entering a business to deduct expenses), Section 41(b)(1) mandates that Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) be paid or incurred "in carrying on" any trade or business of the taxpayer. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(4) addresses how the "in carrying on" requirement applies to research conducted through partnerships and joint ventures, but neither it nor § 1.41-7 codifies the Cleveland decision; rather, under Cleveland's reasoning, outlays a financier makes before a joint venture actually exists are treated as loans to the researcher rather than the venture's research expenditures, and therefore cannot generate § 174A deductions or § 41 QREs for the financier.

body.text: The Fourth Circuit's Final Holding

In a carefully bifurcated opinion, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded the Tax Court's decision. With respect to the pre-April 20, 1956 advances, the Fourth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's disallowance of all deductions claimed for taxable year 1955 ($5,598.42) and all advances made between January 1, 1956, and April 19, 1956. The appellate court held that the Tax Court's finding that Cleveland's advances prior to the execution of the written Trust Agreement on April 20, 1956, were in the nature of loans was not clearly erroneous and was binding on the appellate court. Because the advances were in the nature of loans, the funds belonged to Kerla upon receipt, and any research expenditures made with those funds were paid or incurred by Kerla, not by Cleveland. Furthermore, although the agreement was executed retroactive to December 31, 1954, the Fourth Circuit gave it no retroactive effect, recognizing the joint venture only on and after April 20, 1956, and leaving the earlier advances characterized as loans.

Conversely, the Fourth Circuit reversed the Tax Court regarding advances made on and after April 20, 1956, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. Rejecting the Tax Court's rigid formalism, Judge Boreman held that although neither the term "partnership" nor "joint venture" appeared in the April 20, 1956 Trust Agreement, the effect of its contractual provisions, considered as a whole, was to make Kerla and Cleveland equal participants in a joint venture. Because the agreement required Kerla to devote his full time to active experimentation and to keep accurate records of the funds advanced, required Cleveland to advance the expenses of experimentation insofar as financially able, and provided that the two would share equally in the avails, Cleveland was thereafter engaging with Kerla in the trade or business of promoting the commercial development of the invention, in which he owned a participating one-half interest. Crucially, the Fourth Circuit ruled that executing the agreement specifically to qualify for tax deductions under IRC § 174(a)(1) did not render the contract a sham, holding that the parties' decision to define their legal relationship to claim statutory tax benefits was entirely in harmony with Congress's legislative purpose to encourage research and experimentation. The case was remanded to the Tax Court for further proceedings consistent with the opinion, which held that deduction of expenditures for purposes of experimentation and development made by Cleveland on and after April 20, 1956, should be allowed.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A forensic examination of both the Tax Court opinion (34 T.C. 517) and the Fourth Circuit ruling (297 F.2d 169) reveals a series of severe legal, contractual, and evidentiary failures by the taxpayer. While the Fourth Circuit salvaged the post-April 20, 1956 portion of the 1956 claim, the taxpayer suffered a total loss of the 1955 deduction ($5,598.42) and a partial loss of the 1956 deduction ($3,342.83) due to avoidable structural and documentation errors. In contemporary IRS audits involving IRC §§ 41 and 174A, these exact deficiencies remain primary triggers for disallowance, amplified by modern statutory substantiation mandates.
Failure to Establish a Contemporaneous Qualifying Business Relationship (The Debt vs. Venture Trap)

The primary legal failure that destroyed Cleveland's 1955 and early 1956 deductions was the absence of an enforceable, contemporaneous joint venture or contract research agreement at the time the funds were advanced. Under IRC § 174(a)(1) (and modern IRC §§ 174A and 41(b)), research expenditures are deductible or creditable only by the taxpayer who actually "paid or incurred" them. In Cleveland, absent a formal partnership, joint venture, or research agreement, the Tax Court found as a fact—and the Fourth Circuit accepted as not clearly erroneous—that the advances were loans, and the Tax Court further treated those loans as the purchase price of a one-half interest in the invention.

In a debtor-creditor relationship, the lender transfers cash in exchange for an implied or express promise of repayment. When the borrower (Kerla) subsequently spends that borrowed cash on laboratory chemicals, apparatus, or testing, the expenditure is legally incurred by the borrower, not the lender. Even if the loan becomes uncollectible, the lender's recourse is governed by the bad debt provisions of IRC § 166—not the research expense provisions of IRC § 174 or § 41. By operating on an informal handshake basis for over two decades while advancing thousands of dollars, Cleveland failed to establish the legal conduit necessary to attribute Kerla's experimental activities to himself prior to April 20, 1956.
Inefficacy of Retroactive Contractual Backdating ("As Of" Execution Defect)

Attempting to cure two decades of informality, Cleveland—himself an experienced attorney—and Kerla executed the Trust Agreement on April 20, 1956, but its opening recital and closing attestation stated that the agreement was entered into "as of December 31, 1954". Cleveland contended that he and Kerla had been engaged in a joint venture since at least 1945 and that the written document merely recorded the tenor of their pre-existing mutual understanding, so that the joint venture should be recognized across the entire 1955 and 1956 tax years.

Neither court gave the agreement retroactive effect: the Tax Court found that no joint venture existed at all, and the Fourth Circuit, while accepting the finding that the pre-execution advances were loans, recognized the joint venture only on and after April 20, 1956. Although the Fourth Circuit did not articulate a general rule on retroactive recitals, its holding is consistent with the broader principle of federal tax jurisprudence that, while contracting parties may adjust their private civil rights retroactively as between themselves, retroactive recitals cannot alter the federal income tax consequences of transactions already completed in prior taxable years or prior periods before a legal relationship actually changed. Under Subchapter K (IRC § 761(c)), modifications to an existing partnership agreement may be given retroactive effect for a taxable year if made prior to the statutory due date of the partnership return, but taxpayers cannot retroactively fabricate a partnership's existence for a prior year (1955) after the close of that year when no partnership existed in fact. Consequently, the "as of December 31, 1954" recital was given no effect in determining the deduction, so all 1955 advances and all pre-April 20, 1956 advances remained loans outside the joint venture.
Damaging Testimonial Admissions Regarding Subjective Intent

Under the Supreme Court's holdings in Commissioner v. Culbertson, 337 U.S. 733 (1949), and Commissioner v. Tower, 327 U.S. 280 (1946), the existence of a valid tax partnership or joint venture is a question of fact that depends upon whether the parties, in good faith and acting with a business purpose, truly intended to join together in the present conduct of the enterprise. The burden of proving this contemporaneous intent rests squarely upon the taxpayer.

During questioning at trial by counsel identified in the opinion only as Mr. Seidman, Cleveland made fatal testimonial admissions that undermined any claim of a pre-April 1956 joint venture. When asked whether he ever believed the money advanced to Kerla prior to the written agreement was a loan, Cleveland testified: "I believe in the early days if I had thought of it I would have so regarded it. Again, I can't say at what point — and Mr. Kerla said I was a part owner — when that concept came in in place of the loan concept.". Furthermore, when pressed on how long he had considered himself engaged in the trade or business of developing the patent, Cleveland admitted: "Mr. Seidman, as you are well aware, I didn't think in those technical terms until this case arose under Section 174. But certainly, again, the best I can tell you is that at least 10 years and probably 15 years before 1955.". The Fourth Circuit relied on Cleveland's acknowledgment that he would have regarded the early advances as loans, his admission that "there was nothing enforceable" between him and Kerla, his lack of interest in the amounts Kerla spent on experimentation, and his vague testimony about any change in the relationship, holding that the Tax Court's finding that the pre-April 20, 1956 advances were loans—and thus that the intent required under Tower and Culbertson to operate as a joint venture rather than as lender and borrower had not been shown—was not clearly erroneous.
Commingling of Non-Qualifying Personal Support with Experimental Expenditures

A further evidentiary complication reflected in the record was the commingling of personal living expenses with laboratory development costs, although the parties ultimately agreed on the amounts actually expended for research and experimentation ($4,923.07 in 1955 and $3,234.86 in 1956) and no deduction was claimed for advances used for Kerla's personal living expenses. Beginning shortly after their first meeting and continuing through the tax years at issue, Cleveland provided Kerla with funds both for the personal maintenance and support of Kerla's family (including rent-free occupancy of the house Cleveland purchased in 1946) and for experimental materials and equipment.

In the Tax Court's view, the written agreement made no provision for sharing expenses and liabilities incurred in developing and commercializing the binder, whereas the Fourth Circuit emphasized that the agreement required Kerla to keep accurate annual records of advances and a detailed account of experimental expenditures, to be submitted to Cleveland by February 1 of each succeeding year. While the Fourth Circuit remanded the case to allow deductions for actual experimental expenditures incurred by the joint venture after April 20, 1956, the court's holding was limited to expenditures for purposes of experimentation and development; personal family living allowances were never at issue because Cleveland claimed no deduction for them, and the agreement itself excluded the cost of the house Cleveland purchased from the advances it covered. In modern R&D tax credit examinations, this mirrors the fatal error of claiming general ledger project totals, unallocated overhead, or guaranteed partner draws without granular nexus tying specific wage, supply, or contract dollars to qualified research activities.
The "Trade or Business" and Executive Participation Vulnerability

The Commissioner determined, and the Tax Court upheld, that Cleveland—whose primary occupation and business was the practice of law—did not make the expenditures in connection with his trade or business; although the Fourth Circuit's opinion does not cite it, this position parallels the passive-investor principle of Higgins v. Commissioner (under which personal investment management does not rise to the level of a trade or business regardless of its size or continuity). Cleveland overcame this objection for the post-April 20, 1956 period because the Fourth Circuit construed the written agreement as making the parties equal participants in a joint venture: Kerla agreed to devote his full time to active experimentation on the invention, Cleveland agreed to advance the expenses of experimentation insofar as financially able, and the two were to share equally in the avails, so that Cleveland was thereafter engaging with Kerla in the trade or business of promoting the commercial development of the invention (the record also showed that Cleveland acted as a business advisor, handled legal aspects of proposed transfers of rights in the binder, and introduced Kerla to potential commercial outlets).

However, as subsequent post-Snow jurisprudence and IRS Chief Counsel guidance demonstrate, the Cleveland structure sits on a razor's edge. In cases following Cleveland and Snow, courts have consistently disallowed Section 174 deductions where individuals contribute cash to a partnership that merely funds research performed by an unrelated third-party corporation under a licensing or option agreement, holding that the partnership is a passive investor lacking both the objective intent and capability—the "realistic prospect"—of entering into its own trade or business with the fruits of the research.

Furthermore, as modern Tax Court decisions such as Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), Little Sandy Coal, Inc. v. Commissioner, and Moore v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-20) demonstrate, satisfying the Cleveland joint venture test under § 174/174A does not automatically establish eligibility for the IRC § 41 research credit. Specifically, while Cleveland's commercial promotion and legal work helped prove that the joint venture was engaged in a trade or business under § 174, none of Cleveland's own time or legal/promotional efforts would qualify as Qualified Services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), which strictly limits eligible in-house wages to employees engaged in the actual conduct, direct supervision (immediate first-line technical supervision of researchers), or direct support of qualified research. To claim the § 41 credit today, a Cleveland-style venture must also substantiate the Four-Part Test for each business component—proving technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design, a structured process of experimentation evaluating alternatives based on hard sciences, and adherence to the "substantially all" (80% activity) threshold—while avoiding the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and doctrinal requirement examined in Cleveland v. Commissioner (alongside its contemporary IRC §§ 174A and 41 statutory framework) against the taxpayer's specific legal or evidentiary failures and the governing judicial standard of proof established by the Tax Court and the Fourth Circuit.

headers: Outcome in Cleveland & Modern IRC §§ 174A / 41 Impact

cells: 1. "Paid or Incurred by the Taxpayer" (IRC § 174(a)(1); Modern IRC §§ 174A(a) & 41(b)(1))

Prior to April 20, 1956, Cleveland advanced funds to Kerla on an informal basis without a written joint venture or research contract. The advances operated as personal loans to Kerla, meaning Kerla (the borrower), not Cleveland (the lender), legally incurred the research expenses.

A taxpayer claiming R&E deductions must prove that the expenditures were incurred directly by the taxpayer or by a valid, pre-existing partnership/joint venture in which the taxpayer holds an active interest. Advances structured or intended as loans are non-deductible by the lender.
Disallowed for 1955 & Pre-April 20, 1956; Allowed Post-April 20, 1956. Under modern IRC § 41, loan advances or convertible debt financing never generate QREs for the lender.
2. Prohibition on Retroactive Entity Creation (IRC §§ 761 & 174; Annual Accounting Principle)

Executed the written "Trust Agreement" on April 20, 1956, but backdated the effective date "as of December 31, 1954" in an attempt to sweep all 1955 ($5,598.42) and early 1956 advances into the joint venture.

Contractual backdating ("as of" clauses) was given no retroactive effect in Cleveland: the Fourth Circuit recognized the joint venture only on and after the date the written agreement was actually executed, leaving earlier advances characterized as loans.

Retroactivity Rejected. Only expenditures paid or incurred on and after the actual execution date (April 20, 1956) qualified. Modern § 41 contract research requires written agreements executed prior to performance (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)).
3. Bona Fide Joint Venture Intent (Culbertson / Tower & IRC § 761)

On cross-examination, Cleveland admitted that in the early days, if he had thought of it, he would have regarded the advances as loans, could not identify when the "part owner" concept replaced the "loan" concept, and did not think in "trade or business" terms until this case arose under § 174 (while asserting he had been in the business at least 10 and probably 15 years before 1955).

Under Culbertson and Tower, the taxpayer bears the burden of proving via objective contemporaneous evidence that the parties, in good faith and with a business purpose, intended to join together in the present conduct of an enterprise.

Failed Pre-April 20, 1956; Satisfied Post-April 20, 1956. The April 20, 1956 written instrument objectively proved mutual intent to share profits (50/50) and release Kerla from any obligation to repay experimental expenses (advances for personal expenses remained repayable if Kerla was fully able) from that date forward.
4. Tax-Motivated Contract Structuring (Substance Over Form / Sham Transaction Doctrine)

It was admitted that the primary purpose of executing the April 20, 1956 Trust Agreement was to qualify Cleveland's advances for tax deductions under newly enacted IRC § 174(a)(1). The Tax Court viewed the agreement as merely converting the earlier loans into the purchase price of a one-half interest, creating neither a partnership nor a joint venture.

A written agreement explicitly motivated by a desire to qualify for IRC § 174 benefits is valid and not a sham, provided the parties genuinely intend to be bound by its substantive economic terms (risk sharing, debt release, and profit division).

Taxpayer Prevailed on Appeal (Post-April 20, 1956). Fourth Circuit held that defining a legal relationship to take advantage of § 174 is in harmony with Congress's statutory purpose to incentivize R&E.
5. "In Connection With" vs. "Carrying On" Trade or Business (IRC §§ 174 / 174A vs. IRC § 41(b)(1))

Cleveland's primary vocation was practicing law; the Commissioner determined, and the Tax Court upheld, that the expenditures for the single chemical invention ("Kerloid") were not made in connection with Cleveland's trade or business.

In Cleveland, the Fourth Circuit held that once the written agreement made the parties equal participants in a joint venture, Cleveland was engaged in the trade or business of promoting the commercial development of a single invention, satisfying the "in connection with" test; the separate requirement that venturers have a "realistic prospect" of entering a trade or business derives from later post-Snow case law rather than from Cleveland.

Satisfied Post-April 20, 1956 for § 174. However, for the modern IRC § 41 credit, the taxpayer must meet the stricter "in carrying on" standard (§ 41(b)(1)) or satisfy the joint venture flow-through rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(4).
6. Expense Segregation & Substantiation (Capital/Personal vs. Experimental Outlays)

Cleveland commingled advances for Kerla's personal family support and rent-free housing (in a home owned by Cleveland) with laboratory material and equipment costs. The parties later agreed on the amounts actually spent on experimentation ($4,923.07 in 1955; $3,234.86 in 1956), and no deduction was claimed for personal living expenses; the Tax Court faulted the agreement for making no provision for sharing expenses and liabilities.

Taxpayer must segregate and substantiate actual experimental expenditures from personal living stipends, loan advances, capital property acquisitions, and non-technical commercial/legal promotion costs.

Remanded for Further Proceedings (Allowance of Post-April 20, 1956 Experimental Expenditures). Under modern IRC § 41 and recent Tax Court precedent (Moore; Little Sandy Coal; Phoenix Design Group), failure to segregate non-technical wages, overhead, or routine costs results in total credit disallowance.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how contemporary United States taxpayers and tax advisors must apply the legal principles of Cleveland v. Commissioner alongside modern IRC §§ 174A and 41 jurisprudence, the following two industry case studies examine realistic commercial projects confronting the exact legal, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls identified in the ruling. Each case study details a step-by-step remediation strategy across project governance, contract architecture, technical documentation, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Advanced Materials & Specialty Chemical Joint Venture (Overcoming Informal Financing, Retroactive Contracts, and Expense Commingling)
Scenario and Identified Cleveland Pitfalls

Apex Polymer Ventures, LLC ("Apex"), a Delaware commercial chemical distribution and licensing firm based in Baltimore, Maryland, seeks to commercialize a novel, zero-VOC refractory inorganic composite binder ("SilicaBind-X") being developed by Dr. Elena Vance, an independent materials chemist operating a private laboratory. Beginning in February 2025, Apex's Managing Director begins transferring $35,000 per month to Dr. Vance's personal bank account to cover her personal living stipend, residential laboratory lease, chemical precursors, and testing equipment at a local university. No formal contract is signed in February 2025; instead, Apex records the monthly transfers on its general ledger as "Convertible Research Advances – Vance."

In November 2025, after learning from its certified public accountant about the restoration of immediate domestic R&E expensing under IRC § 174A and the IRC § 41 research tax credit, Apex and Dr. Vance execute a "Joint Development and Trust Agreement" dated "effective as of February 1, 2025." The agreement grants Apex a 50 percent ownership interest in SilicaBind-X, converts all prior 2025 cash advances into equity contributions, and stipulates that Apex's Managing Director will handle all commercial marketing and patent licensing while Dr. Vance conducts the chemical formulation. Apex claims $385,000 in IRC § 174A deductions and includes the full amount in its IRC § 41 QRE calculation for tax year 2025.

Under Cleveland v. Commissioner, an IRS examination will disallow 100 percent of the February through October 2025 advances ($315,000) under both IRC § 174A and IRC § 41. Recording the transfers as "Convertible Research Advances" without a contemporaneous joint venture agreement establishes a debtor-creditor relationship; thus, Dr. Vance (the borrower), not Apex, paid or incurred the expenses prior to November 2025. Moreover, the "effective as of February 1, 2025" backdating clause is legally ineffective to retroactively convert nine months of debt advances into joint venture expenditures or to satisfy Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2), which requires contract research agreements to be entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research. Even for the November through December 2025 period ($70,000), Apex's claim will fail under IRC § 41 because Dr. Vance's personal living stipends, residential lease costs, and Apex's commercial and legal promotion activities are commingled with laboratory material costs, violating IRC § 41(b) and the substantiation standards enforced in Moore v. Commissioner and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner.
Step 1: Restructure Project Governance and Entity Formation Prior to Funding

To satisfy the Culbertson and Cleveland contemporaneous intent test alongside the IRC § 41(b)(1) "carrying on a trade or business" requirement, Apex and Dr. Vance must abandon informal advances and establish a formal tax partnership before any subsequent development funds are disbursed. Prior to initiating Phase II development (or at the exact moment of restructuring), Apex and Dr. Vance must form a dedicated Delaware Limited Liability Company—SilicaBind Technologies, LLC ("SBT")—governed by a written Operating Agreement taxed as a partnership under Subchapter K (IRC §§ 701–761).

To ensure SBT is not disqualified as a passive investment vehicle under post-Snow case law, the Operating Agreement must vest SBT itself with all legal title and exclusive manufacturing, commercialization, and sub-licensing rights to SilicaBind-X. Furthermore, to allow the IRC § 41 credit to flow through to Apex and Dr. Vance under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(4), the Operating Agreement must establish a joint venture in which both members are actively carrying on the venture's business, are entitled to the research results, and explicitly allocate SBT's § 174A deductions and § 41 credits in accordance with IRC § 704(b) substantial economic effect rules. Finally, the parties must establish a bilateral Technical and Commercial Steering Committee that records contemporaneous bi-weekly minutes. While Apex's Managing Director's commercial promotion activities help establish that SBT has an active trade or business (or a realistic prospect thereof under § 174A), the governance charter must strictly separate commercial and legal management from technical R&D execution so that non-qualifying commercial time is never miscategorized as QREs under § 41(b)(2)(B).
Step 2: Re-Engineer Contract Terms and Risk/Rights Allocation

Whether Apex structures the arrangement going forward as a formal Subchapter K joint venture or as a direct Contract Research Agreement between Apex and Dr. Vance's laboratory entity, the contract language must eliminate every trace of Cleveland loan ambiguity and satisfy IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). The parties must eliminate all promissory notes, repayment clauses, and "as of" retroactive effective dates, ensuring that the written instrument states that all capital transfers are irrevocable, non-recourse capital contributions (in a joint venture) or at-risk research fee payments (in a contract research arrangement) effective solely from the date of actual execution.

If Apex elects to contract directly with Dr. Vance's corporate entity rather than forming a joint venture, the Master Research Services Agreement (MRSA) must comply strictly with Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2) and (3). Specifically, the MRSA must be signed and dated prior to the commencement of any laboratory work, must specify that the research is performed on behalf of Apex, and must stipulate that Apex retains exclusive ownership (or a perpetual, royalty-free right to use) all resulting SilicaBind-X formulations, patents, and trade secrets. In addition, payment terms must place genuine financial risk on Apex—such as non-refundable time-and-materials progress payments where Apex bears the full economic loss if the inorganic binder fails to achieve thermal stability—avoiding fixed-price deliverables where Apex could recover payments under state contract law if the product fails.
Step 3: Overhaul Financial Controls and Expense Segregation

To cure the Cleveland commingling defect—where family living support and rent-free housing were blended with laboratory expenses—Apex and SBT must implement strict chart-of-accounts segregation. All venture funds must be deposited into a dedicated SBT corporate bank account rather than transferred to the inventor's personal account. The general ledger must separate outlays into four distinct cost centers. First, Account 5100 (Qualified In-House Research Wages / Guaranteed Payments under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)) must compensate Dr. Vance strictly via W-2 wages or IRC § 707(c) guaranteed payments representing reasonable compensation for technical services actually rendered in conducting bench chemistry, completely eliminating personal family support stipends. Second, Account 5200 (Qualified Research Supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)) must track consumable silicate precursors, catalysts, and destructive testing substrates used directly in laboratory experimentation. Third, Account 5300 (Qualified Contract Research under IRC § 41(b)(3)) must track payments to Johns Hopkins or third-party university testing laboratories for electron microscopy and thermal stress testing, which are eligible at the statutory 65 percent rate (or 75 percent for qualified research consortia). Fourth, Account 6000 (Non-Qualifying Overhead, Facilities, and Commercial Promotion) must isolate laboratory rent, depreciation, patent filing legal fees, and Apex's commercial marketing costs; while certain facility and overhead costs may be deductible under IRC § 174A or § 162, they must be strictly excluded from the IRC § 41 QRE calculation.
Step 4: Implement Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking

Because satisfying Cleveland only opens the § 174A door, SBT must construct a contemporaneous technical substantiation file that satisfies the Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d) and survives scrutiny under Phoenix Design Group and Little Sandy Coal. SBT must define each distinct chemical formulation—such as SilicaBind-X Batch Series 100 for Aerospace Refractory Coatings—as a discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2). Prior to mixing a batch series, Dr. Vance must log a formal Technical Uncertainty Protocol under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3), documenting why available scientific knowledge cannot establish the capability, method, or appropriate molecular cross-linking design required to prevent micro-cracking at extreme refractory service temperatures. Finally, to satisfy the process of experimentation mandate of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), Dr. Vance must maintain dated Electronic Laboratory Notebooks (ELNs) mapping every hour of technical labor and every gram of chemical supply to a specific hypothesis, alternative molar ratio tested, quantitative shear-strength test result, and iterative failure analysis.
Case Study 2: Biomedical Device & Embedded Firmware Consortium (Overcoming Retroactive Agreements, Executive Wage Disallowance, and Substantiation Failures)
Scenario and Identified Cleveland Pitfalls

NeuroPulse Holdings, Inc. ("NeuroPulse"), a medical device commercialization company based in Richmond, Virginia (within the geographic jurisdiction of the Fourth Circuit), partners with BioSense Engineering Group ("BioSense"), a boutique hardware prototyping firm, to develop an implantable closed-loop vagus nerve stimulator ("VNS-Core"). Throughout calendar year 2025, NeuroPulse transfers $1.2 million to BioSense under a series of informal "Bridge Loan Term Sheets" to fund breadboard prototyping and animal trial builds. Meanwhile, NeuroPulse's Chief Operating Officer (COO)—a corporate finance and regulatory executive—spends significant time negotiating hospital pilot sites, managing investor relations, and reviewing high-level project schedules with BioSense's directors.

On March 15, 2026 (prior to filing its 2025 federal corporate tax return), NeuroPulse and BioSense sign a formal "Retroactive Joint Venture and Research Allocation Agreement" dated "as of January 1, 2025," which cancels the 2025 bridge loan notes, establishes an unincorporated joint venture for 2025, and allocates 100 percent of the R&D tax credits to NeuroPulse. On its 2025 Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), NeuroPulse claims $1.2 million in payments to BioSense plus 65 percent of its COO's $400,000 salary ($260,000) as QREs, relying on year-end oral estimates and general ledger project totals.

Under Cleveland v. Commissioner and contemporary Tax Court precedent (Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20; Little Sandy Coal, Inc. v. Commissioner; Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113), NeuroPulse faces total disallowance of its 2025 R&D tax credit claim. Because the 2025 transfers were made pursuant to "Bridge Loan Term Sheets," NeuroPulse was legally a lender throughout 2025. Under Cleveland, executing a joint venture agreement on March 15, 2026—"as of January 1, 2025"—cannot retroactively convert 2025 debt advances into joint venture research expenditures for the closed 2025 tax year. Furthermore, while the COO's commercial and regulatory negotiations mirror Richard Cleveland's promotional activities (which helped prove the existence of a business venture under § 174), under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Moore v. Commissioner (where the Tax Court excluded a COO's wages from QREs for lack of substantiation and because a higher-level manager's oversight is not direct supervision), general management, commercial promotion, and supervising managers who supervise researchers do not constitute "direct supervision" or "actual conduct" of qualified research. Finally, relying on general ledger totals ($1.2 million) without project-level time and supply tracking fails to prove the experimental-activity fraction required under the "substantially all" (80 percent) test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) for the VNS-Core pilot models.
Step 1: Immediate Execution of a Prospective Joint Venture or Consortium Agreement

NeuroPulse must immediately recognize that the 2025 bridge loan advances cannot be retroactively converted into 2025 QREs via the March 15, 2026 backdated document, and must instead restructure the legal relationship to lock in valid deductions and credits from March 15, 2026 forward. Mirroring the legal mechanism the Fourth Circuit validated with respect to the April 20, 1956 agreement in Cleveland, NeuroPulse and BioSense must execute a binding Joint Venture Operating Agreement effective March 15, 2026, that unconditionally releases BioSense from all debt repayment obligations for future advances, pools BioSense's engineering workforce with NeuroPulse's capital and clinical infrastructure, and establishes joint ownership and profit-sharing in the VNS-Core technology. To satisfy the stricter "carrying on" requirement of IRC § 41(b)(1) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(4), the Joint Venture Operating Agreement must explicitly stipulate that both venturers are carrying on the medical device development business jointly and that each venturer holds the unconditional contractual right to exploit the resulting VNS-Core intellectual property in its respective trade or business.
Step 2: Restructure Executive and Technical Supervision Governance

To prevent the disallowance of leadership wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Moore v. Commissioner while preserving the commercial participation required under Cleveland, NeuroPulse must bifurcate its commercial and technical leadership roles. The company must remove the COO's commercial negotiation, hospital site acquisition, and investor relations duties from the IRC § 41 QRE pool entirely, acknowledging that while those activities support the entity's "trade or business" status under Cleveland and IRC § 174A, they are non-qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B). Concurrently, NeuroPulse and the joint venture should appoint a Chief Biomedical Engineer (CBE) who directly and immediately supervises the bench electrical and firmware engineers developing the VNS-Core pulse generator. The CBE must document first-line technical supervision through signed code-review approvals, schematic sign-offs, and daily stand-up engineering directives, supported by contemporaneous project timecards rather than year-end percentage estimates.
Step 3: Implement Sub-Component "Shrinking-Back" and Pilot Model Accounting

To overcome the substantiation failures identified in Little Sandy Coal and Phoenix Design Group regarding complex hardware and software pilot models, the venture must apply the shrinking-back rule and sub-component decomposition under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2). Rather than treating the entire VNS-Core clinical program as a single monolithic business component—where routine titanium casing fabrication or regulatory paperwork could dilute the experimental-activity fraction below the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold—the engineering team must decompose the project into discrete qualifying sub-components: Sub-Component A (Closed-Loop Neural Spike Detection Firmware Algorithm), Sub-Component B (Ultra-Low-Power ASIC Piezoelectric Harvesting Circuit), and Sub-Component C (Biocompatible Hermetic Lead Encapsulation Seal, treated as a Pilot Model under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4)).
Step 4: Deploy Granular Activity-Fraction and Experimentation Tracking

To substantiate the experimental-activity fraction for each decomposed sub-component, the venture must implement an integrated engineering work-order system (such as Jira and Git repositories linked directly to enterprise resource planning cost codes) that tracks every engineering hour and prototype material outlay by specific activity category: Hypothesis Formulation, Simulation/Modeling, Prototype Build for Testing, Iterative Bench Testing, versus Routine Commercial Production/QA. This architecture provides objective, mathematical proof that more than 80 percent of the research activities on each claimed sub-component constitute elements of a structured process of experimentation, supporting the taxpayer's burden of substantiation under modern IRC § 41 case law.

cells: Legal Instrument & Timing
Informal advances or bridge loans followed by a retroactive agreement dated "as of" a prior tax year.
Contemporaneous written Joint Venture Operating Agreement or MRSA executed prior to funding and research performance.
Financial & Debt Characterization
Transfers recorded as loans, convertible notes, or unconstrained personal stipends to the researcher.
Non-recourse joint venture capital contributions or at-risk contract research payments tied strictly to segregated R&D ledger accounts.
Promoter / Executive Involvement
Claiming non-technical legal, commercial, or COO management time as QREs via unsubstantiated percentage estimates.
Relying on commercial promotion solely to prove § 174A trade or business nexus, while restricting § 41 wage QREs to documented bench research and first-line technical supervision.
Technical & Cost Substantiation
Relying on general ledger spending totals and design revisions without proving uncertainty or the 80% experimentation fraction.
Decomposing projects into discrete sub-components supported by baseline uncertainty logs, ELN test matrices, and granular time/supply nexus.

body.text: 5. Synthesis and Strategic Conclusions for U.S. Tax Practitioners

The Fourth Circuit's decision in Cleveland v. Commissioner, 297 F.2d 169 (4th Cir. 1961), remains one of the most instructive opinions in United States research and development tax jurisprudence because it illustrates both the fatal peril of informal pre-contract financing and the judiciary's willingness to respect prospective, tax-motivated joint venture structuring.

For contemporary corporate taxpayers, venture studios, and technical tax advisors operating under IRC §§ 174A and 41, three authoritative legal imperatives emerge from the Cleveland ruling and its modern progeny. First, the execution date of a written research or joint venture instrument operated in Cleveland as the decisive boundary. Federal tax law does not permit taxpayers to rewrite history through retroactive "as of" contract clauses. Any funds advanced to an inventor, university, or engineering group under a loan, convertible note, or informal arrangement prior to the actual execution of a joint venture or qualified contract research agreement are permanently disqualified as R&E deductions or QREs for the financier. Tax counsel must ensure that binding written agreements establishing joint venture status (or satisfying Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)) are executed before the first dollar is disbursed.

Second, explicit tax planning is legally permissible when backed by genuine economic substance. The Fourth Circuit's landmark pronouncement—that defining a legal relationship specifically to qualify for statutory R&E incentives is "in harmony with the purpose of the enactment to encourage expenditure for research and experimentation"—provides a powerful defense against IRS sham-transaction challenges. So long as the written agreement genuinely alters the legal and economic rights of the parties by eliminating debt repayment obligations, pooling technical and commercial contributions, and sharing economic risk and profit, the presence of a tax-reduction motive will not invalidate the structure.

Finally, practitioners must rigorously bridge the statutory gap between Section 174A deductibility and Section 41 credit eligibility. While active commercial and legal promotion by a capital partner helps establish a qualifying trade or business nexus under Cleveland and IRC § 174A, it does not satisfy the rigorous technical and substantiation requirements of IRC § 41. To withstand modern IRS examination and Tax Court scrutiny, taxpayers must pair a Cleveland-compliant legal entity structure with strict accounting segregation of personal and commercial overhead, rigorous exclusion of non-technical executive wages, and contemporaneous, sub-component-level documentation of technological uncertainty and a structured process of experimentation.

metaDescription: Cleveland v. Commissioner (4th Cir. 1961): advances before the joint venture agreement were nondeductible loans; later experimental costs were deductible.
